title: What is the role of leader and follower replicas, and what is the in-sync replica set (ISR)?
shortTitle: Leader and follower replicas and the in-sync replica set (ISR)
topicTitle: What is the role of leader and follower replicas, and what is the in-sync replic

s1_definition.profdef: In Kafka, each partition is replicated across several brokers for fault tolerance. One replica is elected the leader and handles all reads and writes for that partition; the remaining replicas are followers that passively fetch and copy the leader's data to stay current. The in-sync replica set (ISR) is the subset of replicas — the leader plus all followers that are sufficiently caught up with the leader — that are eligible to be promoted to leader if the current leader fails. A write is considered committed once it is acknowledged by all replicas in the ISR, which is what makes Kafka durable.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a transaction ledger in three identical copies in three different branches for safety. One branch is the official branch (the leader) where all new entries are written and all queries are answered; the other two branches (followers) constantly copy every new entry so they match. The set of branches that are fully up to date — the official one plus any copy that is not lagging behind — is the in-sync set. If the official branch burns down, the bank promotes one of the fully up-to-date copies to become the new official branch, and no entries are lost.
s1_definition.oneliner: The leader serves all reads and writes, followers copy it, and the ISR is the caught-up replicas eligible to take over.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Kafka, each partition is replicated across several brokers for fault tolerance. One replica is elected the leader and handles all reads and writes for that partition; the remaining replicas are followers that passively fetch and copy the leader's data to stay current. The in-sync replica set (ISR) is the subset of replicas — the leader plus all followers that are sufficiently caught up with the leader — that are eligible to be promoted to leader if the current leader fails. A write is considered committed once it is acknowledged by all replicas in the ISR, which is what makes Kafka durable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps a transaction ledger in three identical copies in three different branches for safety. One branch is the official branch (the leader) where all new entries are written and all queries are answered; the other two branches (followers) constantly copy every new entry so they match. The set of branches that are fully up to date — the official one plus any copy that is not lagging behind — is the in-sync set. If the official branch burns down, the bank promotes one of the fully up-to-date copies to become the new official branch, and no entries are lost.

**One line to remember:** The leader serves all reads and writes, followers copy it, and the ISR is the caught-up replicas eligible to take over.

sections.s2_technical:
Replication is configured per topic with a replication factor. A replication factor of three means each partition has three copies on three different brokers. Among those copies, Kafka elects exactly one as the leader for that partition. All producer writes and all consumer reads for the partition go through the leader. This single-leader design keeps ordering simple, because there is one authoritative sequence of appends.

Followers do one job: they continuously fetch records from the leader and append them to their own copy of the log, trying to stay as close to the leader's latest offset as possible. Followers do not serve client reads in classic Kafka (though newer versions allow follower fetching for locality). Their purpose is to be ready to take over. The closer a follower stays to the leader, the faster and safer a failover will be.

The in-sync replica set is the heart of Kafka's durability model. The ISR contains the leader plus every follower that is caught up within the allowed lag, governed by `replica.lag.time.max.ms`. If a follower falls behind — because its broker is slow, overloaded, or partitioned from the network — and does not fetch within that time window, the leader removes it from the ISR. When the lagging follower catches up again, it rejoins the ISR. So the ISR is a dynamic set that shrinks and grows with the health of the followers.

The ISR interacts directly with the producer acknowledgment setting. With `acks=all` (also written `acks=-1`), the leader only acknowledges a write after every replica in the current ISR has copied it. Combined with the topic setting `min.insync.replicas`, this gives a strong durability guarantee: if `min.insync.replicas=2` and the ISR shrinks below two, the leader rejects writes rather than risk accepting data that could be lost. This is how a bank ensures a committed transfer survives a broker failure — the write existed on at least two brokers before being acknowledged.

Leader election happens when the current leader's broker fails. The controller picks a new leader from the ISR, because only ISR members are guaranteed to have all committed records. Choosing a leader from the ISR means no committed data is lost during failover. If you enable `unclean.leader.election.enable=true`, Kafka may elect a leader from outside the ISR when no ISR replica is available, trading durability for availability — this can lose data and is normally disabled in banking systems.

The senior-level nuance is the three-way tension between durability, availability, and latency. Requiring `acks=all` with `min.insync.replicas=2` on a replication factor of three means you can tolerate one broker failure and still accept writes, while guaranteeing every acknowledged write is on at least two brokers. Setting acks lower or allowing unclean elections increases availability and throughput but risks data loss. For money movement you choose durability; for high-volume telemetry you might relax it. You also monitor ISR shrink events closely, because a chronically shrinking ISR signals an unhealthy or overloaded broker that threatens both durability and the ability to accept writes.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must guarantee that a committed transfer event is never lost even if a Kafka broker crashes, and the team must model how leaders, followers, and the ISR protect the data.

Problem 1 — A transfer event for Rajesh is written to a partition on one broker. If that broker's disk dies, the event must still exist elsewhere. This is exactly why we replicate the partition and have followers copy the leader.

Problem 2 — The bank must be sure that when Kafka says a transfer is committed, it truly survives a single broker failure. This is exactly the ISR plus acks=all plus min.insync.replicas rule — the write is acknowledged only after it lives on enough in-sync replicas.

Problem 3 — When the leader broker crashes, a new leader must take over without losing any committed transfer. This is exactly leader election from the ISR — only a caught-up replica is promoted.

The mini-project simulates a replicated partition. We build a `TransferEvent` domain object, a `Replica` with a log and a last-fetched offset, a `PartitionReplication` managing one leader and several followers with an ISR computed by lag, and a `ReplicationManager` that writes with acks=all, lets a follower lag and drop out of the ISR, and elects a new leader from the ISR when the leader fails. The demo writes a transfer, shows the ISR, lags a follower, then fails the leader and elects a new one with no data loss.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two transfer events TXF-1 and TXF-2 written to a partition with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2.

Step 1 — The partition starts with leader broker-1 and followers broker-2 and broker-3. None is lagging, so the ISR is all three brokers.

Step 2 — TXF-1 is written with acks=all. The manager checks the ISR size is 3, which is at least the required 2, so it proceeds. The leader appends TXF-1 and every in-sync replica copies it, then the write is acknowledged as committed. TXF-1 now exists on all three brokers.

Step 3 — broker-3 becomes slow and does not fetch within replica.lag.time.max.ms, so it is marked lagging and drops out of the ISR. The ISR shrinks to broker-1 and broker-2.

Step 4 — TXF-2 is written with acks=all. The ISR size is now 2, which still meets min.insync.replicas of 2, so the write proceeds. The leader and broker-2 copy TXF-2 and it commits. broker-3 does not have TXF-2 yet because it is out of the ISR.

Step 5 — The leader broker-1 crashes. The manager elects a new leader from the current ISR, excluding the dead leader, which leaves broker-2. broker-2 is in-sync and has both TXF-1 and TXF-2, so it becomes the new leader with no committed data lost. The ISR now reflects broker-2 as leader. This demonstrates that leaders serve writes, followers copy them, the ISR tracks who is caught up, and failover from the ISR preserves every committed transfer.

```
2026-10-24 20:28:00 [INFO] COMMIT TXF-1 SAV2001->CUR3001 50000 acks=all on ISR [broker-1, broker-2, broker-3]
2026-10-24 20:28:00 [INFO] ISR now = [broker-1, broker-2, broker-3] leader=broker-1
2026-10-24 20:28:00 [WARNING] broker-3 is lagging beyond replica.lag.time.max.ms
2026-10-24 20:28:00 [INFO] COMMIT TXF-2 SAV2001->CUR3001 12000 acks=all on ISR [broker-1, broker-2]
2026-10-24 20:28:00 [INFO] ISR now = [broker-1, broker-2] leader=broker-1
2026-10-24 20:28:00 [SEVERE] broker-1 (leader) crashed
2026-10-24 20:28:00 [INFO] ELECTED new leader broker-2 from ISR — no committed data lost (endOffset=2)
2026-10-24 20:28:00 [INFO] ISR now = [broker-2] leader=broker-2
```

```
  │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ + writeAcksAll(event): void   │  rejects if ISR < minInSync
  │ + electNewLeaderFromIsr()     │
  │ + showIsr(): void             │
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ manages
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │     PartitionReplication      │ 1   1..*│       Replica        │
  │ - leader: Replica             │◆──────▶ │ - brokerId           │
  │ - followers: List<Replica>    │        │ - log: List<Event>    │
  │ + isr(): List<Replica>        │        │ - lagging: boolean    │
  │ + markLagging(broker): void   │        │ + append(event)       │
  │ + setLeader(replica): void    │        │ + endOffset(): long   │
  └──────────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a follower ──────────────────────────────────

  [IN-SYNC (in ISR)] → lags beyond replica.lag.time.max.ms → [OUT OF ISR]
  [OUT OF ISR] → catches up → [IN-SYNC]
  [IN-SYNC] + leader dies → eligible → [PROMOTED to LEADER]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. mgr.writeAcksAll(TXF-1) → isr=3 ≥ 2 → append on all → COMMIT
  2. partition.markLagging("broker-3") → ISR shrinks to 2
  3. mgr.writeAcksAll(TXF-2) → isr=2 ≥ 2 → COMMIT (not on broker-3)
  4. mgr.electNewLeaderFromIsr() → pick broker-2 (in-sync) → no loss

  Contract for writeAcksAll(event):
    Pre:  none
    Post: committed only if ISR copied it AND ISR size ≥ min.insync
    Rule: reject write if ISR too small (durability over availability)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In Kafka, every partition is replicated across several brokers, and among those replicas one is elected the leader while the rest are followers. The leader handles all reads and writes for the partition, which keeps ordering simple because there is a single authoritative log. The followers continuously fetch records from the leader and append them to their own copies, their only job being to stay caught up so they are ready to take over if the leader fails.

The in-sync replica set, or ISR, is the heart of Kafka's durability. It is the leader plus every follower that is caught up within the allowed lag window. If a follower falls behind beyond replica.lag.time.max.ms, the leader drops it from the ISR, and when it catches up it rejoins. The ISR is therefore a dynamic set that reflects the health of the replicas.

The ISR works hand in hand with the producer acks setting and the min.insync.replicas topic setting. With acks=all, the leader only acknowledges a write after every replica in the current ISR has copied it, and if min.insync.replicas is two, the leader refuses writes whenever the ISR shrinks below two rather than risk accepting data that could be lost. When the leader broker dies, the controller elects a new leader from the ISR, because only in-sync replicas are guaranteed to have every committed record, so failover loses no committed data. Unclean leader election, which would promote an out-of-sync replica, is normally disabled in banking because it can lose data.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, I run transfer topics with replication factor three, acks=all, and min.insync.replicas two. That means a committed transfer always lives on at least two brokers before Kafka acknowledges it, we can tolerate one broker failure and still accept writes, and if the leader crashes a caught-up replica takes over with no lost transfers. The senior point I make is that this is a deliberate trade-off between durability, availability, and latency, and for money movement I always choose durability, while watching ISR-shrink alerts closely because a chronically shrinking ISR warns of an unhealthy broker.
